title: Infra: GPU Fleet + Cloud Accounts + IaC + CI/CD Playbook (2026)
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This playbook consolidates operational standards and runbooks for Redwood's infrastructure engineering surface related to GPU fleet and capacity, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform / IaC modules, CI/CD and build pipelines, and day-to-day runbooks used by the infra team. It is intended for oncall engineers, infra owners, and platform engineers who implement or operate model serving capacity.

Scope

- GPU fleet lifecycle: provisioning, capacity planning, tagging, and decommissioning
- Cloud account structure and VPC/networking patterns for inference and control plane services
- Terraform / IaC module design, testing and release patterns
- CI/CD for infra changes including image builds, module publication and infra rollouts
- Runbooks for common incidents (capacity depletion, network partition, failed rollout)

Ownership & contacts

- Primary owner: infra-engineering (oncall: infra-oncall@redwood.example.com)
- GPU fleet lead: Ravi Singh (ravi@redwood.example.com)
- Networking lead: Janelle Kim (janelle@redwood.example.com)
- IaC & CI/CD lead: Diego Morales (diego@redwood.example.com)
- Pager escalation: infra-oncall -> infra-sre -> eng-platform -> CTO (see oncall rota)

High-level architecture

- Control plane (private account): management APIs, deployment controllers, KMS/HSM integrations.
- Serving accounts (per-region): dedicated accounts for hosted inference and dedicated/private deployments.
- GPU pools: tagged compute instances (G5/G6/NX series) in multiple AZs with autoscaling groups and node pools for dedicated capacity.
- Networking: VPC per account, regional peering and Transit Gateway for private deployments.

GPU fleet & capacity management

SLOs and KPIs

- Target p95 token latency for production models: <= 150ms for short prompts (<=512 tokens)
- Capacity SLAs: 99.9% requested capacity available for Reserved (Dedicated) customers; best-effort for Hosted tier
- Queue length target: < 20 requests queued per node for 95% of time
- Utilization bands and thresholds:
  - Green: 0-60% (normal)
  - Yellow: 60-80% (monitor, prepare scale actions)
  - Red: >80% (trigger autoscale policy / capacity request)

Instance selection & tagging

- Preferred instance families: G6 (fp16, int8), G5 where G6 unavailable, and validated A100/NV links for large models.
- Mandatory tags on compute resources: team, service, model-family, cost-center, environment, deployment-id
- Example tags: {team: "platform", service: "inference", model-family: "gpt-*-quant", environment: "prod", deployment-id: "ded-nyc-01"}

Capacity planning cadence

1. Weekly capacity snapshot generated every Monday (automated).
2. Monthly predictive planning based on release calendar and expected usage peaks.
3. Quarterly procurement/commit review for Reserved capacity contracts.

Autoscaling policies

- Horizontal autoscaling for worker pools (preferred): scale out by 25% when p95 CPU/GPU utilization > 70% for 5m.
- Vertical scaling only for test/staging clusters (requires redeploy).
- Burst policy: emergency short-term burst capacity from a shared spot pool (policy requires pre-approval for production use).

Capacity request template

- Use the capacity request template (internal form) with fields: justification, expected start/end, model(s), instance types, region, estimated tokens/day, cost approval id. Attach relevant dashboards and the snapshot output.

Cloud accounts & networking

Account topology

- Organization layout: root -> billing -> prod-control-plane -> prod-serving-{region} -> staging-serving-{region} -> partner / private customer accounts (as needed)
- Least privilege: control plane holds minimal IAM to avoid lateral blast radius. Serving accounts own compute and networking.

VPC and connectivity patterns

- VPC per serving account and region with 3 private subnets (one per AZ), 1 public management subnet.
- Transit gateway for private customer deployments. Use VPC peering for simpler internal services if latency is critical and cross-account traffic is limited.
- NAT Gateway per AZ for egress, Flow Logs to S3 for 90 days.
- Internal DNS zone per account registered in central Route53 / internal DNS service.

Security groups & network ACLs

- Minimal open ports: SSH only from bastion account (no direct public SSH). Ingress for model-serving agents limited to LB and internal control plane.
- Egress: restrict to required endpoints (metrics, S3, KMS, container registry).

Terraform / IaC modules and patterns

Module registry & naming

- Registry: internal Terraform module registry hosted in monorepo packages/infra-modules.
- Module names: short, hyphenated, descriptive (e.g., rg-vpc, rg-gpu-node-pool, rg-autoscaler).
- Module versioning: semantic versions (vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Publish a new release for any breaking change.

Module design principles

- Modules must be small, composable and idempotent. Single responsibility per module.
- Inputs: only required inputs + optional overrides. Avoid environment-specific defaults.
- Outputs: expose resource IDs, primary ARNs, and data required by consumers (e.g., subnet_ids, node_role_arn).
- Use tags and naming conventions by default; allow overrides for customer/private deployments.

Example module usage

- Example (Terraform snippet):

```hcl
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//rg-gpu-node-pool?ref=v1.4.0"
  name_prefix = "ded-nyc-01"
  instance_type = "g6.2xlarge"
  desired_capacity = 8
  min_size = 2
  max_size = 32
  tags = { team = "platform", service = "inference" }
}
```

Testing & CI for modules

- Every module must include integration tests using terratest or kitchen-terraform in a sandboxed non-prod account.
- PRs must pass: static checks (tflint, terraform fmt), unit plan (tf plan), and an optional apply-to-temp-account test for modules touching networking or compute.

CI/CD and build pipelines

Pipeline stages (infra repo)

1. Lint & format (pre-commit hooks)
2. Static analysis (tflint, checkov)
3. Unit plan (terraform init/plan in a clean workspace)
4. Integration tests (terratest) - run in sandbox account via ephemeral credentials
5. Publish module (on tag) to internal registry and update module reference docs
6. Deployment PR: apply to target account via gated pipeline with approvers

Gate & approval policy

- Any change to network modules requires 2 approvers: networking lead + infra release owner.
- Changes that affect global resources (Transit Gateway, DNS) require security review.
- Emergency hotfix flow: create a hotfix branch, run limited checks, and get rapid approval from oncall + lead. Document the rationale in PR.

Image build & artifact registry

- Base images: built from a hardened golden-image pipeline that includes security scanning and SBOM generation.
- Images pushed to internal registry with immutable tags (e.g., platform/gpu-worker:2026.02.28-abc123).

Release and rollout strategy

- Canary first: roll changes to a single AZ or small percentage of node pool (5-10%) for 1-2 hours while monitoring latency and error rates.
- Progressive rollout: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% with automated health gates.
- Automatic rollback if any health gate fails (p95 latency increase >20% or new error rate >0.5%).

Infra runbooks (operational playbooks)

1) Capacity shortage (high severity)

- Symptoms: sustained p95 latency >150ms, queue length rising, autoscaler failing to add nodes.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Acknowledge incident in PagerDuty and create incident channel.
  2. Check autoscaler logs and controller health: `kubectl -n infra logs deploy/autoscaler-controller`
  3. Inspect cluster utilization dashboards (GPU Utilization, queue length, node readiness).
  4. Manually scale node pool if autoscaler stalled:
     - Terraform: update desired_capacity and apply (non-production only) OR
     - AWS CLI (fast): `aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name <asg> --desired-capacity <n>`
  5. If capacity cannot be added in region, initiate cross-region burst routing (route policy: route-to-region: fallback-region) and notify customer-facing teams.
  6. Open capacity request with procurement for longer term.

- Post-incident: run a capacity postmortem and update predictive models.

2) Network partition affecting control plane

- Symptoms: control plane cannot reach serving accounts, deployments failing, API calls 5xx
- Steps:
  1. Validate VPC reachability via `telnet`/`nc` from bastion.
  2. Check Transit Gateway / peering status in console and CloudWatch.
  3. If Transit Gateway route leak suspected, reapply route tables from IaC: `terraform apply -target=module.tgw-routes`
  4. Failover control plane to standby region if outage > 10m (follow DR runbook).

3) Failed rollout (new module or image causes degradation)

- Symptoms: error rates spike post-rollout, latency regressions on model routes
- Steps:
  1. Pause rollout in the pipeline and mark PR as blocked.
  2. Revert to previous image/module by triggering rollback job (pipeline step) or manually apply previous Terraform tag reference.
  3. Run garbage collection on the cluster to remove stuck pods.
  4. Capture logs and collect core dumps for postmortem.

Operational commands & examples

- Inspect GPU utilization (Prometheus query example):
```
avg by(instance) (irate(gpu_utilization_total[5m]))
```
- Check ASG desired/actual sizes (AWS):
```
aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --auto-scaling-group-names <asg>
```
- Quick scale via Terraform (recommended pattern):
```bash
# create a change branch, update variables, run plan and apply in gated pipeline
git checkout -b scale/ded-nyc-2026-03
# update variables.tfvars
terraform plan -var-file=prod-ded-nyc.tfvars
terraform apply -var-file=prod-ded-nyc.tfvars
```

Observability & alerting

Key dashboards

- GPU Fleet Overview (utilization, temperature, memory, pod counts)
- Capacity Planner (predictive usage vs committed capacity)
- Network health (Transit Gateway, peering counters, packet drop)
- Infra Release Dashboard (canary health gates)

Alert thresholds (examples)

- GPU pool high utilization: p95 GPU utilization >80% for 10m -> P1 alert to oncall
- Node readiness failure rate: >3% nodes Unready in 5m -> P1
- Route table change: unexpected route modification detected -> P2 and notify networking lead

Testing & staging guidance

- Sandbox accounts mimic prod with scaled-down pools. All module changes must run integration tests in sandbox resources.
- Use recorded traffic (sanitized) for canary testing in a dedicated canary cluster.

Maintenance, upgrades & decommissions

- Planned maintenance windows: weekly maintenance window Tuesday 02:00-04:00 UTC for non-critical infra. Notify downstream teams 48h in advance.
- Kernel / driver upgrades: test on staging gpu pools, run perf benchmark suite, then stage on single AZ before global rollout.
- Decommission procedure: drain nodes, cordon, migrate workloads, remove IaC resources and keep resource identifiers in bookkeeping for 90 days.

Post-incident & continuous improvement

- Every P1 incident requires a postmortem within 5 business days, including root cause, timeline, and action items with owners.
- Update this playbook when runbook steps change; doc owners must review quarterly.

Appendix: quick references

- Capacity snapshot script: `scripts/gpu_capacity_snapshot.py --region=us-east-1 --output=reports/cap-snap-YYYYMMDD.json`
- Terraform module publishing: `scripts/publish_module.sh rg-gpu-node-pool v1.4.0`
- Contact list: infra-oncall@redwood.example.com, security@redwood.example.com

Related pages & further reading

- See the IaC module registry (internal) and the GPU benchmarking playbook for details on perf tests.
